questions.problem:
$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]
$$

The Wronskian of the vector-valued functions given above is $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, our Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & 5{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{e}^{3t}\cdot 5{e}^{-2t}-0\cdot 0 \\  & =10{e}^{3t-2t} \\  & =10{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]

Consider the system of linear ODEs above, where $t\in R.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ The function $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}7{e}^{-4t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]$

$\,$ The function $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-3}}

questions.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}7{e}^{-4t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(7{e}^{-4t})^{′} \\ (2{e}^{-4t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7{e}^{-4t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6\cdot 7{e}^{-4t}+7\cdot 2{e}^{-4t} \\ -2\cdot 7{e}^{-4t}+3\cdot 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ (-2{e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6\cdot {e}^{t}+7\cdot (-2{e}^{t}) \\ -2\cdot {e}^{t}+3\cdot (-2{e}^{t})\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-20{e}^{t} \\ -8{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6\cdot {e}^{t}+7\cdot {e}^{t} \\ -2\cdot {e}^{t}+3\cdot {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =|\begin{aligned}7{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(7{e}^{-4t})\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-4t} \\  & =7{e}^{-3t}-2{e}^{-3t} \\  & =5{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,c}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.

questions.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent. In this case, they do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-3t \\ 3t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(1-3t)^{′} \\ (3t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-3t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3(1-3t)+(-3)\cdot 3t \\ 3(1-3t)+3\cdot 3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}2(1-3t) \\ 6t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(2(1-3t))^{′} \\ (6t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2(1-3t) \\ 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3\cdot 2(1-3t)+(-3)\cdot 6t \\ 3\cdot 2(1-3t)+3\cdot 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t)^{′} \\ (t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3t+(-3)t \\ 3t+3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6t \\ 6t\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,b) & =|\begin{aligned}1-3t & 2(1-3t) \\ 3t & 6t\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-3t)\cdot 6t-2(1-3t)\cdot 3t \\  & =6t(1-3t)-6t(1-3t) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $b$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system.

Given that $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2$ are solutions of the same system of linear ODEs, compute the Wronskian is $W(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)$ and determine if the set $\left\{ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \mathbf{x}_2(t) \right\}$ is linearly dependent on $\mathbb R.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)$ of two vector-valued functions 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/51774bbcf79f8ab11069a5d7c955f73cd637f8407aa7a600673de0eaf9adb7ea.png)
is defined as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/ed9d2deba98ee27ebe8a183cab45f42a92f2d4f49733fa8a8f7c9acdf6185912.png)

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, our Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}-4{e}^{2t} & {e}^{t} \\ {e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-4{e}^{2t})\cdot (2{e}^{t})-{e}^{t}\cdot ({e}^{2t}) \\  & =-8{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t} \\  & =-9{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in \mathbb R.$

Therefore, the set $\left\{ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \mathbf{x}_2(t) \right\}$ is linearly independent on $\mathbb R.$

Consider the system of linear ODEs above, where $t\in\mathbb R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)$ of two vector-valued functions 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/e61be508e4ad25ed39996a7a924a732290f3c8be7e5e953e01da6ff35c5669f4.png)
is defined as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/ed9d2deba98ee27ebe8a183cab45f42a92f2d4f49733fa8a8f7c9acdf6185912.png)

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/3ac4270c91e71468086149ed819c644c71d59aea898520acc8e5fbf30205985c.png)

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/7d502d9256ace32899ea72f143f3694db8f0531efebf2dbd0c20dc857bd563b5.png) $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+1)^{′} \\ (-4t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -4t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+1\cdot (-4t) \\ -4\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+(-2)\cdot (-4t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}-4t+2 \\ -4{t}^{2}+8t-4\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/c223cfc85f5a1f23006dd9de1775f898731a2cce2b88d1c27c0ab3f4ee238e66.png) $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(2t+1)^{′} \\ (-4t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t+1 \\ -4t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (2t+1)+1\cdot (-4t) \\ -4\cdot (2t+1)+(-2)\cdot (-4t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/2f5d5dd7f1fe1b1a51df2930d780fc11af9a31f8cac9cc9c38f966eb42bc848d.png) $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t)^{′} \\ (1-2t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 1-2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot t+1\cdot (1-2t) \\ -4\cdot t+(-2)\cdot (1-2t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions $\big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(b,c) & =|\begin{aligned}2t+1 & t \\ -4t & 1-2t\end{aligned}| \\  & =(2t+1)\cdot (1-2t)-t\cdot (-4t) \\  & =(2t+1)(1-2t)+4{t}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t \in \mathbb R.$ Thus, since $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in\mathbb R,$ $\big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.
